lines.text: A land of rivers, rainforest and sugar, the only English-speaking country in South America. This is the story of Guyana, from plantations to an oil boom.
In 1763, in the Dutch colony of Berbice, enslaved Africans rose against the plantation owners, and held out for months.
In 1781 a town was laid out at the mouth of the Demerara. Georgetown, the capital, lies below sea level behind its sea walls.
Britain took the Dutch colonies and joined them as British Guiana. After slavery ended, labourers were brought from India to work the fields.
In 1918 Cheddi Jagan was born. A dentist, he would lead the fight for independence, and later become president.
His great rival, Forbes Burnham, would become the first prime minister, and rule for more than twenty years.
In 1929 a national park was made around Kaieteur Falls, one of the most powerful single drops of water in the world.
Clive Lloyd, born in Georgetown, would captain the West Indies to win the first two Cricket World Cups.
In 1966 the colony became the independent nation of Guyana.
In the seventies an American cult built a settlement in the jungle. At Jonestown in 1978, more than nine hundred of its followers died.
Irfaan Ali, born in 1980, would become president in 2020, as oil began to transform the country.
In 2023 Venezuela pressed its claim to Essequibo, two thirds of Guyana, and tension rose across the border.
From sugar fields to offshore oil, Guyana's story has entered a new and uncertain chapter.
